name: Kahn indegree topological sort
definition: For finite directed graph G=(V,E), set d(v)=|{(u,v) in E}|. Initialize queue Q with d(v)=0. Remove v from Q, append it to ordering L, and for each outgoing arc (v,w) set d(w)=d(w)−1; enqueue w exactly when d(w)=0. If |L|=|V| return L; otherwise report a directed cycle.
variables: V vertices, E directed arcs, d remaining indegree, Q queue, L output order
assumptions: Finite fixed graph with valid endpoints; adjacency lists and one count per arc; self-loops are cycles; empty graph has empty ordering
limitations: O(|V|+|E|) time and O(|V|) auxiliary storage; multiple valid orderings possible; a cycle report does not identify all cyclic vertices
failure_conditions: Invalid endpoints or inconsistent arc multiplicities
A nonempty residual graph without a source prevents a complete topological ordering
computation: Scan arcs to initialize indegrees; process zero-indegree vertices in declared FIFO order, scanning each outgoing list once. Check output count and arc ordering.

source.citation: University of Pennsylvania, CIS 1210, Spring 2025, Recitation 7, Kahn’s algorithm, https://www.cis.upenn.edu/~cis1210/current/recitations/fa25_rec_7_sols.pdf (retrieved text; screenshot unavailable). Original Kahn (1962) DOI 10.1145/368996.369025 retained as unverified locator.

application: General graph computation on synthetic or authorised inputs; no empirical benefit claimed.
required_inputs: Finite directed graph with declared vertex order and adjacency lists.
incompatible_methods: Treating a mathematical specification as an implemented or validated algorithm
mechanism_note: Maintains indegree of the unprocessed induced graph. Every nonempty finite DAG has a source; each emitted vertex precedes all its unprocessed successors. If no source remains, following predecessors in the finite residual graph yields a cycle. Distinct from shortest-path and spanning-forest objectives.

name: Tarjan strongly connected components
definition: For directed graph G=(V,E), assign discovery index i(v)=low(v)=next index on DFS entry; push v on active stack S. For each edge v→w, if w is undiscovered recurse then set low(v)=min(low(v),low(w)); else if w is on S set low(v)=min(low(v),i(w)); otherwise ignore. If low(v)=i(v), pop through v inclusive as one component. Start DFS at each still undiscovered vertex.
variables: i discovery index, low DFS lowlink, S unassigned vertex stack, v,w vertices
assumptions: Finite fixed directed graph; valid endpoints; distinct discovery indices; active-stack membership tracked separately from DFS call stack
limitations: O(|V|+|E|) time, O(|V|) auxiliary storage; recursive depth may reach |V|; output component order depends on traversal choices, but partition does not
failure_conditions: Resource limit on stack or discovery counter
computation: Traverse all adjacency lists once; distinguish tree-edge lowlink propagation from on-stack non-tree discovery-index update; ignore completed components and mark popped vertices inactive.

source.citation: Cornell CS 4120 (Spring 2023), Iterative solving, Tarjan’s algorithm, https://courses.cs.cornell.edu/cs4120/2023sp/notes/iterative/index.html. Original Tarjan (1972) DOI 10.1137/0201010 retained as unverified locator.

mechanism_note: The root condition identifies a maximal mutually reachable group; active-stack bookkeeping distinguishes completed components. Floyd–Warshall computes pairwise paths rather than this linear-time partition; Kahn orders the resulting condensation DAG, not the cyclic graph itself.

name: Edmonds–Karp shortest augmenting path maximum flow
definition: For finite directed network G=(V,E), start residual capacities r(u,v)=c(u,v) (zero for absent arcs). BFS from source s to sink t using r>0 finds a minimum-edge path P. Set δ=min_{(u,v) in P} r(u,v), then r(u,v)=r(u,v)−δ and r(v,u)=r(v,u)+δ along P; accumulate F=F+δ from F=0. Stop when t is unreachable; F is maximum flow value.
variables: c nonnegative capacity, r residual capacity, s,t distinct terminals, P shortest residual path, δ bottleneck, F net flow value
assumptions: Finite fixed directed graph, finite nonnegative capacities, exact arithmetic; aggregate parallel arcs by ordered endpoints, omit self-loops; residual representation permits antiparallel arcs
limitations: O(|V||E|²) time after excluding irrelevant isolated vertices, with O(|V|+|E|) initialization and storage using adjacency lists; finite-precision residual tolerances require separate numerical analysis
failure_conditions: Invalid terminals, negative or nonfinite capacities
Overflow or residual arithmetic that violates nonnegativity or conservation
computation: Initialize reverse arcs as needed; repeat BFS and paired residual updates. Terminal reachable set defines a cut whose capacity equals F; certify max-flow value against that cut.

source.citation: MIT 6.854, Strongly Polynomial Flow Algorithms, Scribe Notes #7, §2, https://courses.csail.mit.edu/6.854/21/Scribe/s7-blockingFlows/unit-capacity.html. Edmonds and Karp (1972) DOI 10.1145/321694.321699 retained as unverified locator.

application: General graph computation on synthetic or authorised inputs; no empirical benefit claimed.

mechanism_note: Residual reverse arcs permit cancellation; shortest residual distances do not decrease and each critical arc can recur only O(|V|) times. Different objective and state updates from Dijkstra; the existing general linear-program specification is not this combinatorial procedure.

name: Hopcroft–Karp bipartite maximum matching
definition: Given bipartite graph G=(L∪R,E) and matching M (initially empty), orient unmatched edges L→R and matched edges R→L. BFS from free L vertices finds shortest distance ℓ to a free R vertex. Select an inclusion-maximal collection of vertex-disjoint shortest augmenting paths P_1,...,P_k in the layered graph by DFS, and update M_new=M △ (E(P_1) ∪ ... ∪ E(P_k)). Stop when no free R vertex is reachable.
variables: L,R disjoint vertex sets, E crossing edges, M matching, ℓ shortest augmenting path length, P_i paths, △ symmetric difference
assumptions: Finite unweighted bipartite graph, valid partition and endpoints, simple edges or deduplicated parallel edges; all paths in a phase selected relative to the same initial matching
limitations: O(|V|+|E|√|V|) time using linear-time layered DFS per phase and removal of isolated vertices; O(|V|+|E|) storage. Solves cardinality, not weighted assignment or nonbipartite matching.
failure_conditions: Layer traversal that does not produce an inclusion-maximal disjoint set
computation: BFS builds shortest alternating layers; DFS with per-phase edge cursors and dead-end removal finds disjoint shortest paths. Flip their edges simultaneously, then rebuild layers. Absence of augmenting paths certifies maximum cardinality.

source.citation: Norbert Zeh, Dalhousie University, Algorithms II §7.4.4, https://web.cs.dal.ca/~nzeh/Teaching/4113/book/matching/bipartite_maximum_matching/hopcroft_karp.html. Original Hopcroft and Karp (1973) DOI 10.1137/0202019 retained as unverified locator.

application: General graph computation on synthetic or authorised inputs; no empirical benefit claimed.
required_inputs: Finite bipartite graph with explicit partition and adjacency lists.
incompatible_methods: Treating a mathematical specification as an implemented or validated algorithm
mechanism_note: Each phase increases matching cardinality by k; shortest augmenting distance strictly increases. This is a specialized disjoint-path phase algorithm, distinct from Edmonds–Karp single-path augmentation and Hungarian weighted assignment; related to unit-capacity blocking flow.
